opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'd be careful with "most credit," because deep learning was very much a collective effort. LeCun, Bengio, Schmidhuber's group, and plenty of people whose names don't come up as often all made essential contributions. But if you asked me to pick one person, I'd probably say Hinton, and the reason is persistence as much as any single idea.

He stuck with neural networks through decades when they were deeply unfashionable. In the late eighties and nineties, and again through the 2000s, the mainstream view in machine learning was basically that neural nets were a dead end. Kernel methods and graphical models were where the serious people were. Hinton kept saying, no, learning distributed representations from data is the right path, and he kept working on it when it wasn't helping his career.

There's also how wide his contributions are. He helped popularize backpropagation, worked on Boltzmann machines and deep belief networks, and was involved in dropout. Then AlexNet came out of his lab in 2012, and that was the moment the whole field turned. It wasn't one paper so much as a long line of ideas that kept moving the field forward.

And then there are the people he trained. A huge share of the researchers who went on to build modern AI passed through his group or were shaped by it. That multiplier effect is easy to underrate. Producing great ideas is one thing. Producing the people who produce the next generation of great ideas is another.

So for me it's that mix: being right early, staying conviction-driven when the evidence was still thin and the incentives pointed the other way, and building a community that carried it forward. That's what I find most inspiring. Being contrarian isn't enough on its own. He was contrarian, correct, and patient enough to wait for compute and data to catch up with his ideas.

r001.rationale: The response says Hinton deserves the pick partly because he kept working on neural networks through decades when they were unfashionable and widely viewed as a dead end.

r002.rationale: It lists several contributions and describes a long line of ideas, but does not say that many ideas important to present-day deep learning were already present in Hinton’s early papers.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the thing people underrate about Hinton is not any single result, it's the persistence through a period where the whole field had basically decided he was wrong. For something like two decades, neural networks were considered a dead end. The money went to kernel methods, to probabilistic graphical models, to things that had nice theory behind them. And he just kept going, kept training students, kept building the intuition that if you stack enough of these simple units and give them enough data, something emergent happens.

That matters because science is not just about being right, it's about being right at the moment when nobody agrees with you and still having the conviction to keep working on it. A lot of people had the backprop idea in some form. Rumelhart, Williams, Hinton wrote the paper that made it click for people, but the math existed earlier. What Hinton did was treat it as a research program rather than a trick. He asked what representations these networks learn, why they generalize, what distributed representations even mean. That framing is what let the field survive the winter.

And then look at who came out of his group. Ilya Sutskever, Alex Krizhevsky, the AlexNet moment in 2012 that really kicked everything off. Yann LeCun was a postdoc with him. So much of the lineage traces back to that one lab in Toronto. I have enormous respect for LeCun and Bengio, and they absolutely earned their share. But if you ask who kept the flame alive when it was least fashionable, and who seeded the people who then proved it at scale, I think the answer is Hinton. The field exists in its current form because he refused to give up on an idea for twenty years.

astra-6.text:
I’d give Hinton the most credit because he kept pushing neural networks when almost nobody believed they were going to work. It wasn’t just one breakthrough—it was decades of developing the ideas, training researchers, and keeping that direction alive until computation and data caught up.

And his influence extends through the people he mentored. So you have both his own contributions and this enormous downstream impact. Of course, that doesn’t mean he did it alone. But if I had to pick one person, that combination of conviction, technical contributions, and mentorship would be why I’d pick Hinton.

I’d give Hinton a lot of credit for sticking with neural networks when very few people thought they were going to work. It wasn’t just one technical contribution; it was decades of pursuing the idea, developing methods, and training people who went on to make major contributions themselves.

That said, I’m not sure there’s a clean way to say one person deserves the most credit. Bengio, LeCun, and many others were essential. But if you’re asking why Hinton stands out, I think it’s that combination of technical insight, persistence, and influence on the people around him.
